episode_title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods

stories.topic: The wallet that never comes out
stories.summary: Amit describes the habit many Indian men have of patting one pocket for the wallet and another for the phone before leaving. He still carries his wallet, but since arriving at the shoot location a few days earlier he has not used it once, because he pays for everything by phone. That bothers him, since he and Ajay have always argued that cash is freedom and that demonetisation was an attack on it.
stories.insight: The convenience of UPI is real and immediate. Its costs to freedom are abstract and come later, which is why it gets praised without much examination. That tension frames the whole episode.
stories.quote: I haven't had to take my wallet out. Not once. Not once have I had to give cash.

stories.topic: Six failed UPI payments at a Delhi red light
stories.summary: A Delhi cop stopped Ajay for going through a red light. The cop refused cash and insisted on electronic payment of the fine. Despite perfect internet connectivity, the UPI transaction failed six times in a row and only went through on the seventh attempt, while Ajay sat grumbling about the state of modern India.
stories.insight: A system pushed from the top, with the state forcing its use, has nobody on the hook for the moments it fails. The user is compelled to use it and has nowhere to go when it breaks.
stories.quote: The cop is saying I will not accept the fine in cash. I will only accept it in electronics, and the damn electronics doesn't work.

stories.topic: Even a computer-savvy friend got conned
stories.summary: Ajay's very tech-savvy friend Ayush Patnaik lost 15,000 rupees to UPI fraud. Ajay explains that UPI was designed top-down and never settled who takes responsibility or how consumer complaints get resolved. So when a payer and payee disagree about whether money arrived, there is no real recourse, and fraud has grown at scale.
stories.insight: Systems that grow organically develop consumer-protection and fraud-handling machinery as they go. A designed 'science project' leaves those messy details for later, and ordinary users pay for it.
stories.quote: Now Ayush is as computer savvy as you can get. And if Ayush got conned out of 15,000 rupees, then imagine what happens to dentists and grandmothers.

stories.topic: How the internet beat a government standard (X.25 vs TCP/IP)
stories.summary: Global telecom monopolies, many of them state-owned even in rich countries, jointly designed a networking standard called X.25 and pushed it as the new global standard, and equipment makers fell in line. Meanwhile DARPA contracted researchers, including Vint Cerf, to build a protocol that could survive battlefield conditions by rerouting dynamically when lines went down. Bill Joy and others put TCP/IP into Unix, academics and hobbyists built BSD and later Linux, and TCP/IP beat X.25 as well as the corporate standards from Microsoft and Novell.
stories.insight: The internet itself is the clearest historical case of bottom-up, decentralised engineering defeating a top-down standard backed by governments. India's push for 'digital public goods' replays the losing side of that story.
stories.quote: So the entire internet revolution came by fighting off a government standard.

stories.summary: In the late 90s and early 2000s, PayPal already offered a payment handle like 'Amit at PayPal' with a backend for sending and receiving money, which is essentially the UPI idea. Many Indian exporters receive large sums through PayPal from customers abroad. When PayPal asked the Reserve Bank of India to let it run domestic payments in India, RBI refused. Ajay notes that even today UPI is open to banks only.
stories.insight: The fair comparison for UPI is not cash-only India. It is an India where private and foreign payment players were allowed in. That alternative never existed, so its cost stays invisible.
stories.quote: And the Reserve Bank of India blocked that. Okay, and the counterfactual I want to say to you is that what if the Reserve Bank of India had not blocked that?

stories.topic: Holding out against Aadhaar, and the one-word answer
stories.summary: Amit refused Aadhaar for as long as he could, but eventually had to link it in order to pay his taxes. People often asked him why he minded giving data to the government when Google and Facebook already had it. His answer was always one word: consent. With a private company he accepts terms of use and can delete his account. With Aadhaar he had no choice.
stories.insight: The real distinction is not how much data an entity holds but whether you agreed to give it and whether you can walk away.
stories.quote: With Aadhaar I have no choice. It is a blow to my freedom from the very entity which is supposed to protect my freaking freedom.

stories.summary: Amit recalls that in the case against activist Teesta Setalvad, the state went through her credit card bills, found she had once bought alcohol, and used it against her at a press conference. He raises this to support Rahul Matthan's argument that the state could always gather such data through older channels without Aadhaar. Ajay replies that before Aadhaar the state had to query some twenty separate databases, which at Indian levels of state capability was a real barrier. The two leave open a disagreement on whether Aadhaar lets the state find your bank details.
stories.insight: The state could always snoop. The question is friction, and what changes when a common identifier makes linking databases cheap for a state of low capability.
stories.quote: they actually looked at her credit card bills and figured out that she'd bought alcohol at one point

stories.topic: From dismissive outsider to wanting insiders inside
stories.summary: Amit has always seen himself as an outsider who speaks truth to power and offends every party equally. Partly through conversations with Ajay, which fed into his newsletter post 'Insiders and Outsiders', he concluded he had sometimes been unfairly harsh on people working inside the system. He still draws a hard line at demonetisation, which he once wrote in the Times of India was the largest assault on property rights in human history. Any economist who backed it, he says, failed a permanent litmus test. DPI is different: if it is getting built anyway, he wants good people shaping it.
stories.insight: Outside criticism and inside engagement can coexist. The useful skill is telling which issues demand that insiders speak up and which reward staying in the room.
stories.quote: if DPI is going to be built anyway, if Aadhaar and UPI are going to happen anyway, I would rather have a Viral Shah and a Sanjay Jain and a Rahul Matthan inside the system than outside.

stories.topic: Gordon Lish and the hidden hand in Raymond Carver
stories.summary: While recommending Raymond Carver, Amit notes that much of Carver's writing was done for Esquire under the editor Gordon Lish, who was given a lot of credit for Carver's work. When the two stopped working together, readers could see how much Lish had contributed.
stories.insight: A distinctive literary voice is often partly a collaboration, and good editing can be invisible until it is gone.
stories.quote: And you realize what an important role editing plays in writing.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic (chapters 27 and 28)
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit opens the episode by saying these chapters prompted it.
recommendations.reason: They showed him that the problem with India's digital infrastructure goes beyond isolated issues like Aadhaar coercion: the whole design logic behind the apparatus is flawed. The book also introduces the phrase 'premature state legibility'.

recommendations.item: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
recommendations.creator: Eric Raymond
recommendations.context: Ajay cites it while describing the messy, competitive 'bazaar' of technology, such as rival electronic health record standards in the US. He urges the engineers behind DPI to read it, and Amit seconds it in the recommendations segment.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it critical reading for every advocate of technology monopolies. It explains why progress comes from many competing minds rather than one designed system.

recommendations.item: Cathedral
recommendations.creator: Raymond Carver
recommendations.context: A short story Amit remembered because its title echoes Raymond's essay. He says the connection is verbal, not conceptual.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a masterpiece that 'just kinda blows me away', and says it is free to read online.

recommendations.item: The Collected Stories of Raymond Carver
recommendations.creator: Raymond Carver
recommendations.context: Amit recommends Carver's whole body of work after recommending 'Cathedral'.
recommendations.reason: He ranks Carver among the great short-story writers: minimal, easy and elegant, in some ways a successor to Ernest Hemingway.

recommendations.item: Short Cuts
recommendations.creator: Robert Altman
recommendations.context: Altman's film built from a set of Raymond Carver short stories.
recommendations.reason: Amit was excited because its structure echoed Altman's Nashville. He admits he was a little disappointed, perhaps because of anchoring, since he was comparing it with Nashville and with Carver's original stories.

recommendations.item: Nashville
recommendations.creator: Robert Altman
recommendations.context: Mentioned as the 1975 Altman film that Short Cuts reminded him of.
recommendations.reason: It is one of his favourite films of all time, and he calls it 'just a masterpiece'.

recommendations.item: True Names
recommendations.creator: Vernor Vinge
recommendations.context: One of Ajay's two closing recommendations. He describes it as a short story.
recommendations.reason: It makes you think about identity in a new way. Ajay says that after reading it you will never sign on to state projects that force everyone to have a single Aadhaar number.

recommendations.item: Vitalik Buterin's writings on identity and political philosophy
recommendations.creator: Vitalik Buterin
recommendations.context: Ajay's second closing recommendation. He playfully calls Ethereum's founder 'the great political philosopher Vitalik Buterin'.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls him a deep thinker at the global frontier of rethinking identity. Amit adds that he is 'not just some random crypto guy' but a serious thinker on politics.

recommendations.item: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma, with Ajay Shah as co-host
recommendations.context: Amit mentions it after Ajay recommends Vitalik.
recommendations.reason: All three of them had a long conversation in it, so it is a way into Vitalik's thinking on politics and identity.

recommendations.item: Rahul Matthan Seeks the Protocol (Episode 360 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit refers to it several times when discussing Aadhaar's privacy design.
recommendations.reason: It gives the strongest case from the other side. Rahul argues that the technology is excellent and that privacy is built into Aadhaar's design, which is the view Ajay challenges here.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: The source of the two concepts Ajay leans on most, 'high modernism' and 'state legibility'.
recommendations.reason: 'Please go read' it, Ajay urges. It shows how state schemes to improve the human condition have failed. He offers an alternative subtitle: 'the unintended consequences of state legibility projects'.

recommendations.item: The Narrow Corridor
recommendations.creator: Daron Acemoglu & James Robinson
recommendations.context: Ajay cites it while warning that surveillance technology may tip the balance of power toward the Indian state.
recommendations.reason: It argues that liberty and prosperity depend on a rare balance between state power and a society that pushes back, and that countries can easily fall out of that corridor.

recommendations.item: The UNIX Episode (Episode 32 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers back to it while explaining his faith in open-source development.
recommendations.reason: It tells the bottom-up story of how Unix was built, the model Ajay thinks DPI designers should study.

recommendations.item: Maps Are Magic (Episode 44 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls describing open-source software and OpenStreetMap as genuine public goods in that episode.
recommendations.reason: It gives the correct example of a digital public good, as a contrast with UPI and Aadhaar.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit points listeners to it during the discussion of the term 'public good'.
recommendations.reason: Ajay explains in more depth there how economists define public goods and market failure.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit sends listeners there after Ajay calls MSP and wheat and rice in Punjab and Haryana a past sin.
recommendations.reason: It explains how bad agricultural policy contributes, indirectly, to India's diabetes epidemic.

recommendations.item: Insiders and Outsiders
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: A post from Amit's India Uncut newsletter that he discusses near the end, crediting conversations with Ajay for its clarity.
recommendations.reason: It sets out his changed view that insiders shaping a system can be as valuable as outsiders criticising it.

recommendations.item: Narendra Modi takes a Great Leap Backwards
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His demonetisation-era Times of India column, linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It contains his argument that demonetisation was the largest assault on property rights in human history, which is his litmus test for when insiders must speak up.

recommendations.item: OSI: The Internet That Wasn't
recommendations.creator: Andrew Russell
recommendations.context: Show-notes reading for Ajay's story of TCP/IP defeating the government-backed networking standard.
recommendations.reason: Background history of how a top-down networking standard lost to the bottom-up internet.

recommendations.item: How to make digital payments work
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes further reading.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's own case for how India's payments field should work, in line with his argument for open entry.

recommendations.item: RBI's proposal for a Public Credit Registry
recommendations.creator: Prasanth Regy
recommendations.context: Show-notes further reading.
recommendations.reason: A related example of a state-run database proposed for finance, relevant to the episode's worries about state legibility.

recommendations.item: The collateral damage of regulatory roulette
recommendations.creator: Vivek Ananth
recommendations.context: Show-notes further reading.
recommendations.reason: Further reading on how unpredictable regulation causes damage, connected to Ajay's point that regulation is the core flaw.

recommendations.item: Data localisation in India: Questioning the means and ends
recommendations.creator: Rishab Bailey & Smriti Parsheera
recommendations.context: Show-notes further reading.
recommendations.reason: Further reading on state control over data in India.

recommendations.item: India's Policy Responses to Big Tech
recommendations.creator: Smriti Parsheera
recommendations.context: Show-notes further reading.
recommendations.reason: Background on how Indian policy treats big tech, which matters for the Google-versus-state comparison in the episode.

recommendations.item: Stack is the New Black?
recommendations.creator: Smriti Parsheera
recommendations.context: Show-notes further reading.
recommendations.reason: A critical look at the 'India Stack' approach to digital infrastructure.

recommendations.item: Digital public infrastructure and public value
recommendations.creator: David Eaves, Mariana Mazzucato & Beatriz Vasconcellos
recommendations.context: Show-notes further reading.
recommendations.reason: Another perspective on DPI, useful for setting against the episode's critique.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah on the Dangers of Digital Public Infrastructure (Episode 72 of Brave New World)
recommendations.creator: Brave New World
recommendations.context: Show-notes further reading.
recommendations.reason: Ajay making the same argument about the dangers of DPI on another podcast.

recommendations.item: Exploring Digital Public Goods
recommendations.context: A website linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: A resource on the digital public goods idea whose terminology the episode questions.

core_ideas.concept: What a public good really is, and why UPI and Aadhaar aren't
core_ideas.explanation: Economists define a public good as non-rival and non-excludable. Clean air is the classic case: your breathing doesn't reduce mine, and nobody can stop a newborn from breathing it. Ajay credits Paul Samuelson with the basic theory. Linux and OpenStreetMap qualify as digital public goods. UPI is the property of one corporation, has finite capacity, and is highly excludable, since even non-banks cannot join as full participants. Aadhaar is a government monopoly. Governments are supposed to provide public goods, but something does not become a public good just because the government provides it.
core_ideas.quote: No, just because a government monopoly does it, it doesn't become a public good.

core_ideas.explanation: Calling these systems 'public goods' or 'infrastructure' borrows the moral glow of words that middle-class India cheers for automatically, which makes criticism sound perverse. Ajay calls this Orwellian. He insists on protecting the meaning of technical terms. Amit's position is that everyday language can evolve on its own, but technical terms like 'market failure' or 'public good' must not slide into 'the market didn't give me a red shirt' or 'good for the public'.
core_ideas.quote: How can you criticize a public good? How can you criticize infrastructure?

core_ideas.explanation: This is James C Scott's term for the belief that powerful scientists, engineers, bureaucrats and politicians can design society on a whiteboard and impose the design, either through deference or coercion. The real world is a complicated mix of asymmetric information, fraud, crime and consumers with real problems, and designed systems handle that richness poorly. In plain terms, the label sounds attractive but describes coercion from the top down.
core_ideas.quote: The problem with the high modernist idea is it does not adequately grapple with the messiness of the real world.

core_ideas.concept: No business model makes a 'science project'
core_ideas.explanation: UPI has no revenue model, so every participant is supposed to take part out of nation-building spirit. Private firms will put on a demo and attend the ribbon-cutting, but they won't invest seriously in teams, equipment, consumer protection or continuing improvement without profit. The results are chronic transaction failures, unresolved disputes and widespread fraud.
core_ideas.quote: The only way the heart of a private person can be in it is when there is revenues in it, when there's profit in it.

core_ideas.concept: Single standards are the silence of a graveyard
core_ideas.explanation: Amit puts it simply: the core problem is monopoly, whether state or private, because competition forces a system to adapt or go bust. Ajay adds that standards wars like Betamax vs VHS or TCP/IP vs X.25 are signs of a healthy field, not something to fix. Linux has ten rival file systems, the US has 13 or 14 rival electronic health record systems, and messaging is split across Signal, WhatsApp and Google Chat. Incompatibility is annoying, but private connectors appear to bridge it, and the squabbling drives continuous improvement.
core_ideas.quote: Single standards are mediocrity. Single standards are the silence of a graveyard.

core_ideas.explanation: The modern world is too complex for even the brightest engineers to design. Consumer protection, fraud prevention and the 'hundreds of pages of manuals' have to evolve inside a self-organising system where people pursue their own interests every day. Ajay sees regulation that imposes one central plan as the core flaw. Society's job is to unleash many people searching for solutions, not to have a 'pointy-headed guy at the top' design the Republic.
core_ideas.quote: our job in society is to establish a process of discovery, not design.

core_ideas.concept: State legibility, and premature state legibility
core_ideas.explanation: State legibility, another of Scott's terms, is the state's ability to see its people. Historically, states that gathered information about their people have repeatedly abused it, so every increase in what the state can see needs a matching increase in checks and balances. India issued its first Aadhaar number in 2009 and still has no privacy law in 2024. Unlike countries that carried common-law privacy traditions forward (a policeman can't open my letter, so he can't read my email), India has neither those traditions nor a modern law. Ajay and Kelkar's book calls this 'premature state legibility'. Amit adds that Indians are already 'subjects and not citizens'.
core_ideas.quote: So what you need is a very complex set of check and balance where every time the information in the hands of the state goes up, you need to commensurately increase the checks and balances.

core_ideas.explanation: Defenders say the state could always piece together your profile from many databases. Ajay says that is true in principle, but given how weak India's state capability is, linking twenty databases was a real barrier in practice. A universal ID removes that friction, so database linkage actually happens for the first time. Amit had taken comfort in the state's incompetence, and this argument takes that comfort away.
core_ideas.quote: So under Indian levels of state non-capability, this is a decisive step.

core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Acemoglu and Robinson, Ajay argues that the freedom and prosperity of advanced economies come from a rare balance: a capable state held in check by a society that tells it to 'buzz off'. That balance is not the natural state of affairs. Where the state wins decisively, as in China or Russia, modern technology can keep it on top for good. Ajay and Kelkar ask whether India's surge in state legibility has tipped the balance and created new obstacles to becoming a republic.
core_ideas.quote: It is almost impossible to envision the emergence of the UK of the Renaissance and the Enlightenment coming about in China today.

core_ideas.concept: Why the state is not Google
core_ideas.explanation: Google has no coercive power over you. You can spread your digital life across 20 firms, none of which can subpoena the others. The worst outcomes are a security breach or manipulative targeted ads, and in advanced economies breaches cost companies hundreds of millions of dollars, which pushes them to protect data. The Indian state has coercive power, is not accountable, has weak capability, and is already leaking sensitive datasets. Amit reduces the difference to one word: consent.
core_ideas.quote: Google knows a lot about me, but Google does not have coercive power on me.

core_ideas.concept: Credit the technology, not the monopoly
core_ideas.explanation: The cheers for UPI give a state monopoly the credit for what Moore's Law would have delivered anyway. Ajay's analogy is Air India: early air travel felt miraculous, but that was the magic of aviation, and service improved once rival airlines were allowed in. Had India opened payments to private and foreign players in the 90s, it would have had several rival systems. They would have been somewhat inconvenient, but they would have kept improving.
core_ideas.quote: We are attributing the glory of Moore's Law on electronic payments to UPI. Actually Moore's Law on electronic payments could have come to us by another channel, which is a private competitive industry with multiple rivals.

core_ideas.explanation: Many policies feel great to consumers in the short run and turn out to be toxic. India celebrated the Green Revolution, but the means it used, MSP and wheat and rice in Punjab and Haryana, created costs the country is still paying. A thinker's job is to ask whether the strategic path is right, not just whether it works today.
core_ideas.quote: It was a terrible mistake to set up MSP and to do wheat and rice in Punjab and Haryana and so on, and now we are paying for those sins.

core_ideas.concept: In public life, engineers must also be philosophers
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay respects the idealists who built these systems at great personal cost, but he rejects the defence 'I'm just a plumber, the philosophers failed us'. He blames India's weak tradition of political philosophy, law and thinking about liberty for making silver bullets look exciting. Anyone acting in public space still has to think through how their work affects welfare. Amit extends the duty to everyone with a voice.
core_ideas.quote: when you operate in public space, you don't have a choice. You can no longer be an engineer. You have to be a bit of a philosopher.

core_ideas.concept: DPI is not a development silver bullet
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's closing point: the popular idea that digital payments and identity mark a transformative moment for Indian economic development is mistaken. India's development problems lie elsewhere, and the hype itself shows how weak economic thinking in India is.
core_ideas.quote: there is like nothing about the Indian development crisis which really will be materially moved by these technologies.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: When the crew calls 'Amit rolling' before the take, Amit says: 'it's very easy to get a Bengali like me rolling because an essential condition for that is roundness. And I have a lot of that. I'm trying to lose some of it.'
Ajay uses the old line twice in the episode: 'An economist is someone who, when something works in practice, wonders whether it works in theory.'
Ajay declares 'I'm a Nazi on language... no plebeian evolution of language' and lodges his protest 'in triplicate': 'the Guild of Economists shall not accept such terminology.'
Amit on how technical terms get diluted: 'Oh, the market failed to give me a red shirt, it's a market failure.'

The running card joke. Ajay calls himself a 'card carrying engineer, in addition to being an economist', and Amit asks how many cards he has ('I carry a couple'). Amit later wants him to become a card-carrying political philosopher too, and Ajay sums up Vitalik Buterin as 'the card carrying engineer that turned into a card carrying political philosopher.'
Amit: 'my philosophy is let a thousand flowers bloom, which is why we are wearing these shirts' and adds 'Dil garden garden hoya.'

Ajay, feigning wonder at Air India's early days: 'It's a plane. It's heavier than air. It flies... I got into the plane and in thirty minutes I had reached Bhuj.' His point is that the marvel belonged to aviation, not to the monopoly.
Amit justifies wandering off to Raymond Carver and Robert Altman in an episode about DPI: 'these are payments for the soul.'
Tower of Babel: Ajay warns that if everyone uses technical words in their own way, 'we will get a tower of Babel.'
Paul Samuelson, credited by Ajay with the basic theory of clean air as a public good, which he calls 'one of the great milestones in history.'
Betamax vs VHS, Ajay's example of a classic standards war alongside TCP/IP vs X.25 vs Microsoft's NetBEUI vs Novell NetWare.
DARPA and Vint Cerf: TCP/IP was built to keep working under battlefield conditions. Ajay notes that this design suits the hills of Himachal Pradesh, where lines keep going down and coming back up.
Orwell and the panopticon: Ajay calls the 'public goods' language Orwellian, and Amit calls the DPI apparatus a panopticon being built around Indians.
